claims.text: Short-duration, low-temperature rapid annealing after deformation enhances atomic bonding at lamellar interfaces.
Rapid post-deformation annealing relieves residual interfacial stresses.
Enhanced bonding and interfacial stress relief reduce microcrack initiation at dual-phase lamellar boundaries.
Rapid post-deformation annealing improves room-temperature tensile ductility.
Rapid post-deformation annealing improves tensile strength.
Eutectic high-entropy alloys can have a fine lamellar microstructure containing fcc and B2 phases.
Internal lamellar boundaries serve as microcrack-initiation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation.
A high heating rate and very short annealing duration can selectively produce localized diffusion along lamellar interfaces.
A narrow annealing window can promote interfacial diffusion without significantly coarsening grains or altering the lamellar architecture.
Localized interfacial diffusion heals incipient defects that would otherwise nucleate microcracks.
Maintaining the dual-phase lamellar architecture preserves high strength.
Increasing boundary cohesion reduces crack propagation and thereby increases ductility.
Annealed samples will have a statistically significant reduction in lamellar-interface microcrack density relative to the deformation-only baseline.
Annealed samples will have greater room-temperature tensile elongation than the deformation-only baseline.
Annealed samples will maintain or slightly increase tensile strength relative to the deformation-only baseline.
Conventionally deformed eutectic high-entropy alloys typically have high strength but limited ductility because of microcracking at weak lamellar interfaces.
Increasing annealing temperature can cause grain coarsening.
Excessive annealing time or temperature can deteriorate the lamellar structure and negate the mechanical-property improvements.
The magnitude of strength and ductility changes may depend on alloy composition and initial microstructure.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis asserts that strength will improve, whereas the predicted outcome permits strength merely to be maintained and the falsification rule requires only that strength not decrease. Thus, no strength gain could satisfy the experiment even though it would fail the stated simultaneous-improvement hypothesis.
